Left-sided heart failure primarily affects the lungs, causing dyspnea and pulmonary edema, while right-sided heart failure leads to systemic venous congestion, manifesting as peripheral edema and hepatosplenomegaly.

qs.q: Autopsy findings of a patient with chronic left-sided heart failure reveal heavy, boggy lungs and the presence of hemosiderin-laden macrophages. What are these specific cells commonly called?
qs.e: Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages found in the lungs of patients with chronic left-sided CHF due to extravasation of red blood cells from increased pulmonary pressure. Foam cells are lipid-laden macrophages found in atherosclerotic plaques.

qs.q: A patient with long-standing left-sided heart failure develops secondary right-sided heart failure. Upon gross examination of the liver at autopsy, what characteristic appearance is most likely to be observed?
qs.e: Right-sided heart failure causes centrilobular congestion in the liver, giving it a gross appearance known as nutmeg liver. Portal hypertension and chronic congestion can eventually lead to cardiac cirrhosis rather than a cobblestone pattern.

qs.q: Which morphological change is commonly found in the heart during the advanced stages of chronic ischemic heart disease or long-standing left-sided heart failure?
o: Hypertrophy limited strictly to the cardiac atria
Thinning of the pericardial sac exclusively present
Isolated right ventricular atrophy with thinning
Left ventricular hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis
qs.e: Chronic left-sided heart failure and ischemic heart disease morphologically present with left ventricular hypertrophy, dilation, and interstitial fibrosis. The atria do not undergo isolated hypertrophy without ventricular involvement in standard left heart failure.

qs.q: What microscopic finding in the lungs is characteristic of chronic left-sided heart failure?
qs.e: Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages found in the lungs resulting from extravasated red blood cells due to increased hydrostatic pressure. They are a classic morphological feature of left-sided heart failure.

qs.q: A patient with left-sided heart failure develops severe shortness of breath and frothy pink sputum. The primary mechanism driving this pulmonary edema is:
o: Lymphatic obstruction in the pulmonary hila
Increased capillary permeability from direct alveolar injury
Decreased plasma proteins due to hepatic congestion
qs.e: Left heart failure raises pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing fluid into alveolar spaces through a purely hydrostatic mechanism. Permeability remains largely unchanged in uncomplicated hydrostatic pulmonary edema.

es.q: A critically ill patient develops sudden severe dyspnea, hypoxemia refractory to oxygen, and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, without evidence of primary left-sided heart failure. Identify the clinical syndrome and its histological hallmark.
es.m: The clinical syndrome described is Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), which develops from Acute Lung Injury (ALI). Its histological hallmark in the acute phase is Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD), characterized microscopically by hyaline membranes, capillary congestion, and alveolar flooding.

ai.summary: Left‑sided heart failure is a failure of the left ventricle to pump blood efficiently, causing pulmonary congestion and reduced systemic output. It is most often due to ischemic heart disease or hypertension.

sections.p: Left‑sided heart failure occurs when the left ventricle cannot eject blood adequately, leading to increased pulmonary venous pressure and pulmonary congestion. Diagnosis combines clinical signs, imaging, and biomarkers.

t.b: Is the patient experiencing heart failure? High levels (>125 pg/mL) suggest HF, especially when symptoms are present.
Is the left ventricle pumping efficiently? EF <40% confirms systolic HF; 40‑49% indicates mid‑range HF.
Does the lung show congestion? Kerley B lines, interstitial edema, or pleural effusion support HF.

sections.p: The New York Heart Association (NYHA) classifies functional limitation, while the ACC/AHA stages (A–D) describe disease progression and prognosis.
b: ACC/AHA A–D: risk, symptoms, structural changes

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, the top causes are ischemic heart disease, hypertension, rheumatic valve disease, and infectious myocarditis.

sections.p: Patients report dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Physical exam shows tachycardia, S3 gallop, and pulmonary crackles.

sections.p: Rapidly worsening dyspnea, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, and renal failure are urgent complications.
Treat the underlying cause, then support circulation and relieve congestion. Drug choice balances efficacy and safety in low‑resource settings.

faq.a: Dyspnea on exertion appears before orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.

faq.q: Why is an S3 gallop significant?
faq.a: It indicates increased filling pressures and is a marker of systolic dysfunction.
